files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Tell me about the company you work for. What does it make, and who does it sell to?

files.speaker: You
files.text: I work for a textile firm near Hama. We weave and finish cotton fabric, mostly for home textiles — sheeting and curtain fabric. We are about forty people in one workshop, with a small sales office in Damascus. A little over half of what we make is sold inside the country, to wholesalers in Damascus and Aleppo, and the rest is exported, almost all of it to Jordan. I work on the export side, so I deal with the buyers there.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: What happens between a client placing an order and the goods arriving?

files.speaker: You
files.text: First we confirm the order in writing — the quantity, the price and the date — because an order is not an order until those three are agreed. Then the yarn goes to our dyer, who is a subcontractor, and that is usually the slowest step. When it comes back we weave and finish it, which takes a few days. The warehouse makes it up into pallets, and a courier takes it from the border. We raise the invoice on the day we dispatch, and the client pays thirty days from that date.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Tell me about a time something was delayed. What did you do?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Last month our dyer had to stop for maintenance, which put a Jordanian order four days late. I told the client the same day rather than waiting, because if she hears it from us she can plan, and if she hears it from the delivery she cannot. I gave her the new date and said what we were doing about it — we moved the order to the front of the queue and put extra staff on. I also told her when I would know more, and I kept to that. She was not pleased, but she was not surprised either.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Is it better to be the cheapest supplier or the most reliable one? Why?

files.speaker: You
files.text: I think reliable, in our market. A cheap supplier who is two weeks late costs the buyer more than the discount, because they have shops waiting for the fabric. We are not the cheapest and we say so. What we promise is that the date we give is the date, and if it changes we tell the buyer before they ask. That is why our clients come back, and a client who comes back is worth more than one good price. But I would say the price still has to be close. Reliable and expensive is not a business either.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Before anyone says anything, let me put the whole plan on the table, and then I want to be argued with.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: The proposal is that we raise prices by eight per cent from the first of March.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: The reason is the yarn. Our raw cotton has gone up by about fourteen per cent since September and we have absorbed all of it. Our margin on the light weight is now under nine per cent, which is thinner than it has been in four years.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: If we do this, I am going to write to every regular client in the second week of February, so nobody finds out from an invoice. That is three weeks' notice.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: There is a risk, and I want to name it myself rather than have someone else name it for me. Cedar Linens has not placed a first order yet, and an increase lands badly on a buyer who has not bought from us before.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: So the second part of the proposal is that any quotation already issued is honoured at the old price, for its full validity. That costs us something in February and it is worth it.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Right. That is the plan. Who disagrees?

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Can I disagree with the timing rather than the increase? I think the increase is right.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Please.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: March the first is three weeks after we write. For a domestic wholesaler that is plenty. For Jordan it is not, because their season buying is done in February. They will read a March increase as a February increase, and they will bring orders forward to beat it.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Which would be good for February and bad for March.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Exactly. We would be busy for a month and then empty. I would rather we went from the first of April for export clients and the first of March at home.

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: I am not sure I agree with splitting it. Two prices in two markets means two price lists, and when a Jordanian buyer asks why their neighbour pays less, we have no good answer.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: That is fair. Although they are not neighbours — they are in different countries and they already pay different freight.

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: True. I still think one date is simpler, but I take the point about the season.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Fadi, you have not said anything.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: I was waiting. If export orders come forward into February, the workshop cannot take them. We are already running a double shift on the Amman order and the dyer is behind.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: So the plan Samer is worried about creates a problem you would have to solve.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Yes. And I would rather know now than in February.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Good. Then let me put it differently. First of April for export, first of March at home, and Fadi gets a say on any February order above a thousand metres.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: I am happy with that.

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: One more thing before we close. What do I tell Cedar Linens? They have a quotation at the old price, valid until the end of the month, and they have not decided.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Tell them nothing about the increase until the quotation expires. It is honoured at the old price for its full validity, so the increase is not relevant to the decision in front of her.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: And if she asks directly whether prices are going up?

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Then you tell her the truth, and you tell her that her quotation is protected. Never lie to a buyer about a price. They find out, and then every other number you have ever given them is in doubt.

files.text: Can I have that in writing? Not because I doubt it — because I will be the one invoicing her in April.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: I will put the whole thing in a note this afternoon. Anything else? Then we will do that.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: What are your plans for the next few months at work?

files.speaker: You
files.text: We are going to raise our export prices by eight per cent from the first of April. That is decided — raw cotton has gone up about fourteen per cent and we have absorbed all of it so far. Before that, I am going to write to every regular client in February, because I would rather they heard it from me than from an invoice. We may also look at buying our own dyeing plant, but that is only a possibility. Nothing has been agreed on it yet.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: What do you think will happen to prices in your industry this year?

files.speaker: You
files.text: I think they are going to keep rising, at least until the summer. The reason is the cotton price, which has gone up for five months running, and nothing I can see is going to reverse that before the next crop. Transport has become more expensive as well. What I am less sure about is whether buyers will accept it. Some will absorb it and some will look for a cheaper supplier. I would expect the market to divide rather than simply follow.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision at work. What did you do?

files.speaker: You
files.text: My manager proposed raising prices from the first of March, and I thought the increase was right but the date was wrong. So I said that first — that I was disagreeing with the timing and not the increase — because most of her plan was fine and I did not want to argue about all of it. Then I explained that our Jordanian clients buy in February, so a March date would pull orders forward and leave us empty afterwards. She accepted it. We went to April for export clients and kept March at home.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Is it better to promise a date you might miss, or to refuse to give one?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Neither, if you can avoid it. What I would rather do is give the date with its condition attached — four weeks if the yarn arrives Thursday, and I will tell you on Thursday either way. The buyer gets something to plan with and I have not promised what I cannot control. A flat refusal loses orders, because somebody else will give her a number. And a date you miss costs more than the order, because the next time you give one she will not believe it.

files.text: Mr Haffar, thank you for your quotation. Before I put it to my manager I want to check three things.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish

files.text: One last thing. Your quotation does not say what happens if the dye house is late again.

files.text: How do you check whether what a supplier tells you is true?

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: When do you ask a colleague for help, and how do you ask?

files.speaker: You
files.text: My rule is that if I have tried the same thing twice and it has not worked, I stop and ask. The third attempt is almost never the one that works. When I ask, I bring three things: what I have already done, what it produced, and the one thing I want the other person to do. That usually takes three sentences. What I try not to do is apologise first or explain the whole history, because both of those make the person listen less by the time I get to the actual question.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: How do you tell a client that something is going to be late?

files.speaker: You
files.text: As soon as I know, not when I know the new date. That is the part people get wrong, including me once. If I wait until I am certain, the old date has usually already passed and the client finds out from their own calendar. So I write the day it slips, give both dates, say in one clause what caused it, and say what we are doing about it. And I promise another update on a particular day whether or not there is news, because a client who only hears from me when things are good learns to be frightened of silence.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: When something goes wrong, is it better to explain why or just to fix it?

files.speaker: You

The explanation should be one clause, not a paragraph — enough that they know you understand the cause, short enough that it does not read as an excuse. files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: How do you go about chasing a late payment?

files.speaker: You
files.text: I start by assuming it is a process problem rather than a decision, because it usually is. The first reminder is neutral — it names the invoice, offers an innocent explanation, and asks one question. I do not use the word overdue until the second one. If two letters produce nothing, I telephone, because a letter cannot find out that there is a query nobody told us about. That is what happened on our last difficult invoice: two written reminders got silence and one phone call found a two-hundred-metre discrepancy raised three weeks earlier.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Have you ever had to tell a client they were right and you were wrong?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Yes, last month. They said we had invoiced two hundred metres more than we delivered, and I checked the delivery note against the loading record and they were right. I wrote the same day and said so without hedging, because a half-admission would have cost me the credit I got for conceding properly and the money would have been the same. I also told them their query had been raised three weeks earlier and had never reached me, which was our failure. They paid the rest that week.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: How do you put an idea to a group of colleagues?

files.speaker: You
files.text: As a question, usually — could we or what if we — because an idea offered as a question can be turned down without anyone having lost an argument. I try to name the obvious weakness in my own idea before somebody else does, which costs a clause and buys more credibility than the idea itself. And if somebody else has a better one, I say so and say why. Backing another person's suggestion is rarer than making your own, and in a meeting it is worth more.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Is it ever worth losing a customer over a late payment?

files.speaker: You

A client who is consistently sixty days against thirty-day terms is different — they are using us as a bank, and they have not asked. What I would do is say that out loud and agree new terms, rather than chase every invoice forever. Losing them should be the end of a conversation, not the result of never having one.

files.text: Two minutes on something that looks like a small habit and is not.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: When somebody gives you instructions, say them back. Not all of them — the three or four that matter. It takes about eight seconds.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: The reason is not politeness. It is that you cannot tell the difference, from the inside, between having understood and having followed. They feel identical while someone is talking.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Saying it back is the only cheap test. If you can produce it, you have it. If you stumble, you do not, and you have found that out while the other person is still in the room.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: In March we lost nineteen hours on loom three. Two of the four stoppages were never passed on. In both cases the handover was written and not spoken, so nobody said anything back and nobody noticed that the message had not landed.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: There is a second benefit and it is the one people miss. When you say it back, the other person hears their own instruction from outside their head, and about one time in five they correct themselves.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: So: three or four items, in your own words, out loud. And if there were four and you can only remember three, say that too. Asking which one you have lost is not a weakness.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Writing it down feels like checking, though. That is what makes it dangerous.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Yes. Writing captures the sound of a sentence. Saying it back tests the meaning, which is a different thing entirely.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Then you have got it wrong eight seconds after being told, in a room with the person who can fix it, instead of at two in the morning on your own. That is not embarrassment. That is the system working.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: How do you hand work over to someone else?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Three things, and I say how many before I start, so they know how many to hold on to. What was finished, what was started and not finished, and what they must not do. The third is the one people leave out and it is the only one that prevents a mistake rather than describing one. Then I ask them to say it back. It takes about eight seconds and it is the only way to find out whether the message landed, because understanding and following feel the same from the inside.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Tell me about a time a message went wrong at work.

files.speaker: You
files.text: A colleague took a telephone instruction to hold a credit note until a quantity was confirmed, and wrote it down as issue it once the quantity was confirmed. At speaking speed those two sound almost identical and they mean opposite things. She had written it down carefully, which is what made her confident, and writing it down is not the same as checking it. The client was credited twice. If she had read the sentence back, it would have been stopped in two words.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Have you ever proposed a change at work? What happened?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Yes. Our rota had no overlap between shifts on two days of the week, and both of the stoppages we failed to pass on last month happened on exactly those days. So I proposed a fifteen-minute paid overlap on Tuesdays and Thursdays. What I think made it work was putting the cost next to the benefit in one sentence: about forty hours a year against nineteen lost in a single month. Without that it would have read as a complaint about the rota.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Is it better to give instructions in writing or in person?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Both, and for different reasons. Writing survives the shift and can be read at four in the morning by someone who was not there. Speaking is the only version where anything gets checked, because the other person can say it back and you can hear what they did not get. The mistake is thinking that writing it down is checking it. It captures the sound of the sentence, not the meaning, and the one time I have seen a message come out backwards, it was carefully written down.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: How do you approach a negotiation about price?

files.speaker: You
files.text: I try never to concede anything without it buying something. If a buyer asks for a lower price, the answer is not yes or no — it is yes, if you commit to this volume . The shape is always the same and using it every time trains the other side to expect it. I also decide in advance which single thing I will not move on, and I say that one plainly. In my experience if you declare exactly one immovable clause, nobody argues about it. If you declare four, everything is negotiable.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: What do you look for when you read a contract?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Not the commercial terms, usually — those were agreed before the document arrived and they are easy to check. I look for three procedural clauses. Which document wins if two disagree, because that decides every later argument. Whether they can hand the contract to somebody else without asking me, because that could be a competitor. And whether there is any time to fix a problem before it becomes terminal. A contract with no remedy period makes one late delivery enough to end the relationship.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: How do you find out a procedure you do not know?

files.speaker: You
files.text: I ask the person at the counter, and I ask differently from most people. I say why I am asking — that I have been sent away before — so it is worth their time. Then I read the whole list back and ask whether that is all of it, which is where they add the thing nobody thinks to ask about. And I always ask what happens if something is wrong, because the expensive rules live in the failure case. The last time I did that I learned that a pen correction voids a document.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Is it better to agree things on the telephone or in writing?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Agree on the telephone, confirm in writing, and never rely on the telephone afterwards. Most contracts contain an entire agreement clause, which says the document replaces everything said before it, so a promise made on a call is worth nothing once that is signed. The call is where the trading happens, because you can hear hesitation and you cannot in an email. But if it is not in the document, it does not exist, and I write the summary the same day while both of us still remember it the same way.

files.text: How has your company changed over the last few years?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Two things changed permanently. We used to dye our own cloth on site, and that plant closed in 2019 when power costs made it uneconomic; the dyeing has been subcontracted ever since. And we used to run two shifts, which we have not done since 2021. The third change is different — our market mix moved. Iraq used to be about a third of sales and is now under ten per cent, with Jordan taking its place. We have been rebuilding capacity since 2022 and utilisation has gone from sixty-two per cent to seventy-one.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: How do you report a problem to your manager?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Four things, always in the same order. What happened, with a number in it — four cut-outs, twenty minutes each, not it keeps cutting out . What it has cost so far, even when the answer is nothing, because that tells her how fast to move. What it will cost if nothing changes, which is the part most people leave out and the only part that makes anyone act. And what I have already done and what I want from her. If I bring those four she can decide in under a minute.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Tell me about a time keeping a record helped you.

files.speaker: You
files.text: We had a generator cutting out and nobody could say how often, so nothing happened about it. I had been logging the running hours since January, more out of habit than for any reason. When I finally looked at the log, three of the four cut-outs had been after two in the afternoon. That gave us a fix that cost nothing: move the dyeing to the mornings until the generator is serviced. Without the log it was an impression, and an impression does not change anybody's schedule.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: How much should a company tell a customer about its own difficulties?

files.speaker: You
files.text: The part that affects them, in plain words, and not more. If our dye plant closed and that added three days to every lead time, a buyer needs to know the three days. They do not need four paragraphs about why it closed. What I would avoid is both extremes — pretending nothing happened, which a visit to the workshop disproves, and dramatising it, which makes a buyer wonder whether we will still be here next year. Plain, dated and specific, with a number that shows the direction.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: What makes a meeting useful?

files.speaker: You
files.text: An agenda that went out beforehand, with each item marked for what it needs — decision, discussion or information. People prepare differently when they know which it is. Then a chair who closes each item rather than letting it drift, and who is willing to say that nothing is going to be decided today. And minutes within two days that record decisions rather than discussion, with a name and a date on every action. The thing that wastes most time is not long discussions; it is items coming back a second time because nobody wrote down what happened to them.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Have you ever taken minutes? What did you learn?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Yes, for about two years. What I learned is that minutes record what was decided, not what was said. Nobody ever reads a transcript, and a decision with no record gets taken again six months later. Almost every minute I wrote was one of three shapes: a decision in the passive, so it belongs to the room rather than to whoever argued for it; an action with a name and a date; or a line saying an item was discussed and nothing was decided, which stops it coming back as though it had been settled.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: How do you find your way in a building you have never visited?

files.speaker: You
files.text: I tell the person at the desk that I have not been there before, which changes the version of the directions I get. Then I say them back — floor, direction, door — and I keep the negative, because directions almost always contain one thing to avoid and that is the part people drop. I ask what to do if the person I am meeting is not there, which usually produces somewhere better to wait than a corridor. It takes about forty seconds and it means I arrive once instead of twice.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Should everything be written down, or do some things work better spoken?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Decisions and actions get written down, always, because memories differ within about a fortnight and nobody argues with a document circulated two days afterwards. What I would not write down is who argued for what. Minutes that record positions make people careful about speaking, and a meeting where people are careful about speaking is a meeting that produces nothing. So the rule I use is that the outcome is written and the discussion is not. The one exception is when nothing was decided, and then I write that down too.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: A short thing about meetings, and then I will stop talking about meetings for a while.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: There is a difference between having a view and having a position, and most of us stop at the first.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: A view is I think paper records are safer . A position is I would keep paper for declarations only, for seven years, and I would check once a year that the scans still open .

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: The difference is three things: a scope, a cost, and what you would do on Monday morning. A view has none of them.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: The reason it matters is that a room full of views cannot decide anything. Two views are a disagreement. Two positions are a choice, and a choice can be made.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: You are allowed to be wrong. I have changed my own position twice this year, both times because somebody put a better one beside it.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: And if you genuinely do not have one, say that rather than producing a view to fill the silence. I do not know enough to have a position on this is a real contribution, and it is rarer than a bad position.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: The auditor's observation about retention. Do we scan everything, keep paper, or both? Positions, not views.

files.text: Why declarations?

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: Because they are the only documents signed by a named person, and the only ones an authority asks for directly. Everything else can be reconstructed from the two documents either side of it.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: So we have one position with two amendments to it. Lina's, with Samer's dispatch timing and Fadi's constraint about who does it.

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: I am happy with that. It is better than what I came in with.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Then that is the decision. Lina owns the procedure, Samer the scanner, and the yearly check goes in the April agenda every year from now.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Separate the personal data, which the auditor asked for anyway, and keep the rest until each file reaches seven years from its own consignment date. That means nothing is destroyed on one day.

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: I would add one thing. Write down why we destroyed each batch and when, because an empty space in a file is exactly what we were told not to leave.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Both of those go in. Samer, that is the second time today you have turned a question into a position in one sentence.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Why does your company keep records?

files.speaker: You
files.text: So that we can show how something was done, not only so that it was done. An audit trail is the chain of documents that lets somebody start at a payment and work backwards to the order that produced it, and one missing link breaks everything above it. That is why we never correct a document by hand: two versions that cannot be told apart are worse than one that is wrong, because nobody can see which was used. And if a document is missing, we write that in the file. A recorded gap can be explained; a silent one looks like concealment.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Tell me about a time an audit or an inspection found something.

files.speaker: You
files.text: We had a sample check last March, ten consignments out of about two hundred. It found two things: in two cases we could not produce a signed delivery note, and our reissued invoices did not record who had authorised them. We accepted both without arguing, because both were true. The useful part was the root cause on the first one — nobody owned the chase, so nothing was ever overdue to anybody. We put a name against it and a thirty-day period, and the number outstanding halved within two months.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: How do you contribute to a discussion where you have no strong opinion?

files.speaker: You
files.text: I say so, which is rarer than it should be, and then I offer whatever I do know. In our last discussion about scanning I had no view at all on scanners, but I knew that nobody in the workshop would ever scan anything, so whoever did it had to be in the office. That ruled out half of what the room might have decided. A constraint is often worth more than an opinion, and producing an opinion just because the room has gone quiet wastes everyone's time including mine.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Is it ever right to sign something you are not sure about?

files.speaker: You
files.text: No, and our rule says so in four words: if you are not certain, do not sign. A customs declaration is signed by name by the person who prepared it, and that signature says the figures are right, not that somebody told you they were. What makes the rule work is the second half of it — asking has to be safe. If people are blamed for delays caused by checking, they will stop checking, and then the signature means nothing. So the delay is mine to explain, not theirs.

files.text: Walk me through what happens between the cloth coming off the loom and leaving you.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: A short thing about credit, because we are about to rewrite a procedure and I want the right names on it.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Most credit is given badly, and not out of meanness. It is given as a compliment when it should be given as a record.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: A compliment is well done, the report was much clearer . A record is Fadi split the defects from the non-conformances, and that is why the report is clearer .

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: The difference is three things: the name, the specific thing done, and why it mattered. A compliment has none of them, and it evaporates by Thursday.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Say it in front of other people, not privately. Credit given privately is a kindness. Credit given in the room is a record, and a record is what somebody can be promoted on.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Expect the person to deflect. Almost everybody says I only did what the procedure says , and the answer to that is to point out that the procedure allowed it and most people do not do it.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: And one rule for me as much as for you. If you do not know who did it, ask before you thank anybody. Thanking the wrong person is worse than thanking nobody, because the right person is usually in the room.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Shade is forty-six per cent of our faults. We are not here to fix dyeing today. We are here to decide whether the inspection procedure is written well enough to catch it, and to say who wrote which part.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: The procedure is written well. The problem is that step two is written well and performed badly. Sampling across the run is the rule and the bench makes end-sampling the easy thing.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: That is a position. What would you do?

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Make the sheet record where each piece came from, with a position in metres, so that end-sampling leaves a trace.

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: The sheet already records position. Fadi added that field in March, after the audit, and it is the reason we can answer the client at all.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: I only added a column.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: You added the column that makes step two checkable. Before it, the procedure said sample across the run and nothing in the world could tell whether anybody had. That is not a column.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Then my proposal is already done and I would like to know why end-sampling still happens.

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: Because nobody reads the positions back. The field is filled in and never looked at. A record that is never read is not a control.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: That is the finding. What would you do about it?

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: Once a month, take ten sheets at random and check that the positions are spread. It takes twenty minutes and it tells us whether step two happened.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: I would rather it was not me who checked. I filled the field in. Somebody who did not should read it.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Agreed, and that is the better of the two things you have said today. Lina reads them, Fadi fills them, and the separation is the point rather than an insult to either of you.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: One more thing, which is about the client and not about us. Marwan found the shade fault on the Levant Home batch by resampling when the first set looked even. That is in no procedure anywhere.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Then write it in. Not as a rule, because a rule would be ignored. Write it as a note under step two: if a sample looks unusually uniform, take a second one.

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: And put his name on the note, in the revision history. People read the history.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: His name goes on it. So: Fadi owns the position field, Lina owns the monthly read-back, Samer tells the client we have changed the procedure and why, and Marwan's note goes under step two with his name against it.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: I came in wanting to add something that was already there, which I should have checked.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: You came in with the right diagnosis and the wrong fix, and the room produced the right fix in about four minutes. That is what the meeting is for.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Can I ask something? Will the revision history say I added the column in March?

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: It will say it now. It should have said it in March, and that is mine, not yours.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: Fadi added that field in March, after the audit, and it is the reason we can answer the client at all.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: I only added a column.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: You added the column that makes step two checkable.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: That is the better of the two things you have said today.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: Marwan found the shade fault by resampling when the first set looked even.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: And put his name on the note, in the revision history.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: It should have said it in March, and that is mine, not yours.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Describe a process you are responsible for.

files.speaker: You
files.text: Woven cotton is inspected after finishing and before dispatch. The batch is booked in, the customer specification is drawn from the file, and five per cent is sampled at random across the full width and length — never from one end, because a run can drift. Each piece is measured for shade against the approved swatch, and for width, weight and weave. The results go on the inspection sheet with the position each piece came from. Anything outside tolerance is classified: shade faults for rework, weave faults for scrap. Then the supervisor signs and records the reason.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: How do you know a procedure is actually being followed?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Because something it produces can be read back. We had a step that said sample across the run, and for years nothing in the world could tell whether anybody had. Fadi Nassar added a field for the position each piece came from, and that made the step checkable for the first time. Even then the field was filled in and never looked at, which is not a control — a record nobody reads is just paper. So now ten sheets a month are drawn at random and the positions checked for spread, and the person who reads them is not the person who fills them in.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Tell me about a contribution a colleague made that you were able to build on.

files.speaker: You
files.text: Marwan Dib resampled a batch because the first sample looked unusually uniform, and the second one had a shade fault in it. The procedure allowed that and did not require it, and almost nobody does it. We were able to turn it into a note under step two: if a sample looks unusually uniform, a second one is taken. It is written as a note rather than a rule, because a rule to resample whenever cloth looks even would be ignored within a month. His name is on the revision history, which is the part people actually read.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Should a supplier tell a client about a fault it has already corrected?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Yes, and our procedure makes it compulsory before the decision is reached rather than after it. The instinct is to wait until you know what you are going to do, and the cost of waiting is that the client learns you knew first. We were able to change that with one clause: above two per cent the batch is held and the customer is told the same day, whether or not a decision has been reached. It reads as a small thing. What it really does is remove the excuse that we were still looking into it.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: What is the minimum order and why does it exist?

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: A buyer asked for 1,200 metres. Can we do it?

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: What does prices held for twelve months actually commit us to?

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Why do we send the inspection sheet when nobody asks for it?

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: The buyer wants to know our rework rate. Do we tell him?

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: I still do not see why the July lead time is different.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: I have just explained the price hold to Fadi. How do I know it landed?

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: He got it slightly wrong. Do I correct him in front of the buyer?

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Can you just write it down for me?

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: I do not want to look stupid in front of the buyer.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Should I explain the whole procedure or just this part?

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Why are you explaining this to me and not to Samer?

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: If a buyer rings while you are away, what do I actually need to know?

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Four things, and one reason for each. Price: three forty a metre for sheeting, three ninety for pillowcase cloth.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Held for how long?

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Twelve months from award. The reason that matters is that we buy cotton twice a year, so one purchase falls inside the period at a price we cannot see yet. We accepted that knowingly.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Minimum order?

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Two thousand metres a line, because a dye bath below that will not hold shade across the run. If somebody asks for less, you can offer a sample run at a surcharge. Do not just say no.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: And lead time.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Four weeks from order, except July, which is six. The dye house closes ten days in July, so the order waits for the bath and not for the loom. Say it that way and nobody argues.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: What is the fourth thing?

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: The inspection sheet goes with every consignment. Nobody asked for it. It lets the buyer see whether the sample was spread across the run, which no other document shows.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Can I write all that down?

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: You write it and I will check it. If I write it, it is in my words and you will ring me anyway.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Then tell me one more thing. What do I say when I do not know?

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: That you will confirm the figure and come back within the hour. Never guess at a number a buyer might write into an order.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: The coarse cotton is for sacking, not for sheets.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: The dyeing takes two hours in a single bath.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: We order our stationery from a supplier in Damascus.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: The principal reason for the delay is the dye house.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: The principal reason is the lead time in July.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: Of course we can supply the coarse grade as well.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: The dyeing was finished before the cloth was inspected.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: We order stationery twice a year from Damascus.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: It is a matter of principle and not of price.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: The last of these, and it is the one I get wrong most often myself.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: When somebody asks you how something works, there are two things you can give them. You can give them the answer, or you can give them the answer and the reason behind it.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: The answer alone is faster and it comes back to you. Two thousand metres minimum: he can repeat that. He cannot defend it, so the first buyer who pushes sends him to find me.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Two thousand metres, because a dye bath below that will not hold shade across the run: now he can answer a question I have not thought of.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: The second thing is the test, and it is not asking whether they understood. Everybody says yes to that, including when the answer is no. The test is whether they can say it in their own words to somebody else while you listen.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Which brings me to writing. When somebody asks me to write it down for them, I say: you write it and I will check it. It sounds unhelpful and it is the opposite. Writing it is where you find out what you did not understand.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: And give people the sentence for not knowing. I will confirm that figure and come back to you within the hour. Say it out loud a few times until it is available under pressure, because the alternative is a guess, and a guess on the telephone becomes a number on an order.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: One last thing. Explain the part they need, plus one reason. Not the whole procedure. Forty minutes of the whole procedure and they keep the part they came for anyway.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: A hundred points. Forty price, twenty-five quality, fifteen lead time, ten references, ten additional offers. Where do we spend the next two days? Positions, please.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Price. It is the biggest number on the chart and the only one fully under our control.

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: I disagree, and not about the chart. Price is scored against the lowest compliant tender, proportionally. A three per cent cut costs us three per cent of revenue on every metre for twelve months and buys a sliver of forty points.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: What would you do instead?

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: Spend the two days on the sample length and the certification, which is the whole of the quality score. Twenty-five points, and ours is the better cloth. We should be winning that criterion by a distance and we have never once prepared a sample properly.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: That is a better answer than mine and I want to test it. How do you know ours is the better cloth?

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: Because Levant Home moved to us from Aleppo Weaving two years ago and the reason they gave was shade consistency. That is a fact about a buyer's decision, not an opinion about our looms.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: Can I say something about the lead time? I do not have a position, I have a constraint. If we offer four weeks for eleven months, somebody is going to take an order on the twenty-eighth of June and it will land in the July closure.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: That is worth more than a position. What would prevent it?

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: A rule that any order taken after the fifteenth of June gets the July lead time, whatever the calendar says. Written in the tender, not in our heads.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Then my position changes. Price stays where it is, I will write Fadi's June rule into the lead-time section, and the two days go to the sample.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Before we agree that. Additional offers: ten points, and the document says they only score if they reduce the client's own work. Anybody?

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: The inspection sheet. We already produce it. It costs us nothing and it saves a housekeeping manager working out whether a bad consignment was inspected.

files.speaker: Fadi Barakat
files.text: I would not offer the monthly quality report. It is three hours of my time and somebody has to read it, which is their work and not less of it.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Agreed, and that is exactly the distinction the document draws. So: Lina owns the sample and the certification, Samer owns price and the June rule, Fadi's inspection sheet is the additional offer, and the monthly report is dropped.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: One thing nobody has raised. The references. Ten points, scored on being contactable and relevant.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Go on.

files.speaker: Samer Khoury
files.text: Ms Sayegh has agreed to take a call, and I have told her what we claimed about lead time so she answers the right question. The second reference is the hotel in Tartous, and I have not asked them yet. I will do it today, because a reference who is surprised is worse than no reference.

files.speaker: Lina Al-Masri
files.text: And can we write down why we are not cutting the price? Next year somebody will look at this file and think we were being proud.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: Write it down. One line: a three per cent cut buys roughly one point and costs twelve months of margin.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: Where do we spend the next two days? Positions, please.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: That is a better answer than mine and I want to test it.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: How do you know ours is the better cloth?

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: I do not have a position, I have a constraint.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: Written in the tender, not in our heads.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: Then my position changes.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: I have told her what we claimed about lead time so she answers the right question.

files.speaker: narrator
files.text: And can we write down why we are not cutting the price?

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: How do you decide whether to tender for something?

files.speaker: You
files.text: I read two things before anything else. First the mandatory requirements, because a tender that fails one of them is not scored at all — not ranked, not read. Second the weightings, because they tell me what the client is actually buying. On the Barada tender price carried forty points and everything else sixty, which meant a discount was close to worthless and our sample length was worth two days of work. If the weights are all on price and we are not the cheapest workshop in the country, I would rather decline early and say why.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Tell me about a proposal you were involved in.

files.speaker: You
files.text: We tendered for bed linen for a six-hotel group this summer. My part was the lead-time section, and the useful thing in it was not the four weeks — it was the sentence saying we could not hold four weeks through July, and proposing six. A colleague found the real trap: an order taken on the twenty-eighth of June would land in the closure, so we wrote a rule that anything after the fifteenth gets the July figure. We put that in the tender rather than in our heads. I would rather be believed in eleven months than admired in one.

files.speaker: Nour Haddad
files.text: How do you explain something to a colleague so that they can use it?

files.speaker: You
files.text: I give the figure and one reason, and nothing else. Two thousand metres minimum is repeatable; two thousand metres because a dye bath below that will not hold shade is defensible, and the second one survives a buyer pushing back. Then I test it, and not by asking whether they understood — everybody says yes to that. I ask them to say it to somebody else while I listen. If they ask me to write it down, I say: you write it and I will check it. Writing it is where you find out what you did not understand.

files.speaker: Rana Darwish
files.text: Is it ever worth telling a client something that weakens your own proposal?

files.speaker: You
files.text: Almost always, if they would find it out anyway. Our July closure was going to be discovered either by us in the tender or by them in July, and the second version costs a contract rather than a point. Saying it also makes the other eleven months believable, which is the part nobody expects. What I would not do is volunteer a weakness nobody will ever meet, because that is not honesty, it is just a worse document. The test I use is simple: will this reach them later? If yes, it goes in now, in my words.
